q: On January 1, Year 1, Crane Co. issued $500,000 of 10-year, 8% bonds with interest payable annually on December 31. The bonds were issued for $462,090 to yield 10%. Crane uses the effective interest method. What amount of interest expense should Crane report for Year 1?
exp: Under the effective interest method (ASC 835-30), interest expense = carrying amount x market rate = $462,090 x 10% = $46,209. $43,791 is the straight-line result ($40,000 cash + $37,910 discount / 10), which is not acceptable when it differs materially.

q: On January 1, Year 1, Pine Corp. issued $500,000 of 10-year, 8% bonds (interest paid annually each December 31) for $462,090 to yield 10%. Using the effective interest method, what is the carrying amount of the bonds on December 31, Year 1?
exp: Interest expense $46,209 ($462,090 x 10%) less cash interest $40,000 = discount amortization $6,209; $462,090 + $6,209 = $468,299. $465,881 adds straight-line amortization of $3,791 instead of effective interest amortization.

q: Ward Co. issued $1,000,000 of 6% bonds at 100 on April 1, Year 1. The bonds are dated January 1, Year 1, and pay interest semiannually on January 1 and July 1. What total cash did Ward receive from the bondholders on April 1?
exp: Bonds sold between interest dates are sold plus accrued interest since the last interest date: $1,000,000 x 6% x 3/12 = $15,000, so cash = $1,015,000. The purchaser gets it back as part of the full $30,000 semiannual payment on July 1; $1,030,000 wrongly adds a full six months of interest.

q: Under current U.S. GAAP, how should a company present debt issuance costs (underwriting and legal fees) incurred to issue a 10-year term bond?
choices: As a deferred charge (noncurrent asset) amortized straight-line over the bond term
As an expense in the period the bonds are issued
As a reduction of additional paid-in capital
As a direct deduction from the carrying amount of the debt, amortized to interest expense
exp: ASC 835-30-45 requires debt issuance costs on term debt to be presented as a direct deduction from the debt's carrying amount, like a discount, and amortized as interest expense. Showing them as a deferred-charge asset was the pre-ASU 2015-03 treatment.

q: Lowe Corp. reacquired its outstanding bonds (face $1,000,000; net carrying amount $980,000) on the open market at 102 and retired them. How should Lowe report the reacquisition?
choices: Loss of $20,000 in income from continuing operations
Loss of $40,000 in income from continuing operations
Gain of $20,000 in income from continuing operations
Loss of $40,000 reported as an extraordinary item
exp: Reacquisition price $1,020,000 ($1,000,000 x 102%) exceeds the net carrying amount of $980,000, so a $40,000 loss is recognized in income currently (ASC 470-50). Extraordinary-item presentation was eliminated by ASU 2015-01, and $20,000 ignores the unamortized discount.

q: Tern Co. is in financial difficulty. Its note payable has a carrying amount of $550,000 (principal $500,000 plus accrued interest $50,000). The creditor agrees to forgive the accrued interest, reduce the principal to $400,000, and charge 5% annual interest for the remaining 3 years. What gain on restructuring should Tern recognize?
choices: $0, because no gain is recognized on a modification of terms
exp: In a troubled debt restructuring by modification (ASC 470-60), the debtor recognizes a gain only to the extent the carrying amount exceeds total undiscounted future cash flows: $400,000 + ($400,000 x 5% x 3) = $460,000; $550,000 - $460,000 = $90,000. $150,000 ignores the future interest payments.

q: Hale Co., in financial difficulty, settled a $450,000 note payable by transferring land with a carrying amount of $300,000 and a fair value of $360,000. What amount should Hale report as gain on restructuring of debt?
exp: The land is first remeasured to fair value, giving a $60,000 gain on disposal of the asset; the restructuring gain is the debt's carrying amount less the fair value transferred, $450,000 - $360,000 = $90,000 (ASC 470-60). $150,000 lumps both gains together.

q: Vega Inc., which applies current GAAP (ASU 2020-06), issued $1,000,000 of convertible bonds at par. The conversion option is not required to be bifurcated as a derivative, and the bonds were not issued at a substantial premium. What amount should Vega credit to additional paid-in capital at issuance?
choices: $0; the full $1,000,000 is recorded as a liability
An amount equal to the intrinsic value of the conversion feature
The fair value of the conversion option, with the residual allocated to the debt
$1,000,000, because conversion is expected
exp: ASU 2020-06 eliminated the cash-conversion and beneficial-conversion-feature models, so such convertible debt is accounted for as a single liability with no equity component. Allocating a portion to equity reflects the superseded separation models.

q: Dorn Co. issued 1,000 bonds ($1,000 face each) with one detachable warrant per bond for total proceeds of $1,064,000. Immediately after issuance, the bonds without warrants had a fair value of $980,000 and the warrants had a fair value of $140,000. What amount should Dorn credit to additional paid-in capital - warrants?
exp: Proceeds are allocated by relative fair values (ASC 470-20): $1,064,000 x $140,000 / $1,120,000 = $133,000. $84,000 is the incremental (residual) method, used only when just one fair value is known.

q: Bondholders converted bonds with a face amount of $1,000,000 and unamortized premium of $40,000 into 20,000 shares of $10 par common stock under the original conversion terms. Using the book value approach, what amount should be credited to additional paid-in capital?
exp: On conversion per original terms, the bond carrying amount ($1,040,000) is transferred to equity with no gain or loss: common stock $200,000 (20,000 x $10) and APIC $840,000. $800,000 ignores the unamortized premium.

q: On January 1, Year 1, Rook Co. acquired equipment by issuing a $100,000 non-interest-bearing note due in 3 years. The equipment's cash price was not determinable, and Rook's incremental borrowing rate was 10% (present value of $1 for 3 periods at 10% = 0.7513). At what amount should the equipment be recorded?
exp: When a note with no stated interest is exchanged for property whose fair value is not determinable, the note and asset are recorded at the present value using an imputed rate (ASC 835-30): $100,000 x 0.7513 = $75,130. Recording at face overstates the asset and omits $24,870 of interest.

q: A company elects the fair value option for its fixed-rate notes payable. During the year the notes' fair value decreases, part of which is attributable to a deterioration in the company's own credit standing. Where should the portion of the change caused by instrument-specific credit risk be reported?
choices: In net income as part of interest expense
As a direct adjustment to retained earnings
It is not recognized until the notes are settled
In other comprehensive income
exp: Under ASC 825-10-45-5 (added by ASU 2016-01), changes in the fair value of a liability under the fair value option that result from instrument-specific credit risk are presented in OCI; the remaining change goes to net income. Reporting it all in net income was the prior rule.

q: Kerr Co. has a $2,000,000 note payable due March 1, Year 2. On February 10, Year 2, before the December 31, Year 1 financial statements were issued, Kerr issued $1,500,000 of 10-year bonds and used the proceeds and $500,000 of cash on hand to retire the note on March 1. What amount of the note should be excluded from current liabilities on the December 31, Year 1 balance sheet?
exp: A short-term obligation is excluded from current liabilities to the extent the entity demonstrates intent and ability to refinance on a long-term basis, here by issuing long-term debt after the balance sheet date and before issuance (ASC 470-10-45-14). Only the $1,500,000 refinanced qualifies; the $500,000 paid from current assets stays current.

q: At December 31, Year 1, Lark Co. violated a covenant on its 5-year bank loan, making the loan callable on demand. Before the financial statements were issued, the bank waived its right to demand repayment for more than one year from the balance sheet date, and it is not probable that Lark will violate the covenant again within that year. How should the loan be classified at December 31, Year 1?
choices: Current, because it was callable at the balance sheet date
Current, with disclosure of the waiver
Noncurrent
Split equally between current and noncurrent
exp: Under ASC 470-10-45-11, callable debt remains noncurrent if the creditor waives or loses the right to demand repayment for more than one year from the balance sheet date and a recurring violation within 12 months is not probable. Classifying it as current ignores the waiver obtained before issuance.

q: Bonds were issued at a premium and are amortized using the effective interest method. Over the life of the bonds, how does the periodic interest expense behave?
choices: It increases each period
It decreases each period
It remains constant each period
It equals the cash interest paid each period
exp: Premium amortization reduces the carrying amount each period, and interest expense is the market rate times that declining carrying amount, so expense decreases. Increasing expense describes a discount bond, and a constant amount describes straight-line amortization.

q: On January 1, Year 1, Ober Co. issued $1,000,000 of 5-year zero-coupon bonds for $620,921, a 10% annual yield. Using the effective interest method, what is interest expense for Year 2?
exp: Year 1 interest $62,092 brings the carrying amount to $683,013; Year 2 interest = $683,013 x 10% = $68,301. $75,816 is straight-line ($379,079 / 5), and $62,092 is the Year 1 amount.

q: Fenn Co. issued $200,000 of 3-year, 6% bonds paying interest semiannually when the market rate was 8%. Present value of $1 at 4% for 6 periods is 0.7903; present value of an ordinary annuity of $1 at 4% for 6 periods is 5.2421. What were the bond proceeds (rounded)?
exp: Price = $200,000 x 0.7903 + $6,000 x 5.2421 = $158,060 + $31,453 = $189,513. $220,965 uses the annual $12,000 coupon with semiannual factors, and $158,060 omits the interest annuity.

q: Glen Corp. has $800,000 of 9% bonds outstanding with interest payable each April 1 and October 1. What amount of interest payable should Glen report on its December 31 balance sheet?
exp: Interest accrued from October 1 to December 31 = $800,000 x 9% x 3/12 = $18,000. $36,000 is a full semiannual payment, and $54,000 accrues nine months from April 1.

q: Under ASC 835-30, how may a company present debt issuance costs incurred to obtain a revolving line-of-credit arrangement?
choices: Only as a direct deduction from outstanding borrowings, even if nothing has been drawn
As an asset amortized ratably over the term of the arrangement, regardless of borrowings
As an expense when incurred
As a reduction of stockholders' equity
exp: ASU 2015-15 permits costs of a line-of-credit arrangement to be deferred as an asset and amortized ratably over the arrangement's term, whether or not there are outstanding borrowings. The direct-deduction rule applies to term debt and would be awkward when nothing is drawn.

q: Mast Co. maintains a bond sinking fund, held by a trustee, to retire bonds that mature in 8 years. How should the sinking fund be reported on Mast's balance sheet?
choices: As cash and cash equivalents within current assets
As a reduction of bonds payable
As a current asset because it consists of marketable securities
As a noncurrent asset (long-term investments)
exp: A sinking fund restricted to retiring long-term debt is classified like the debt it will retire, so it is a noncurrent asset, usually in long-term investments. Assets are not offset against the debt because the company has not been legally released.

q: Quill Co. placed risk-free U.S. Treasury securities in an irrevocable trust whose cash flows will exactly service its outstanding bonds. The bondholders have not legally released Quill from the obligation. How should Quill account for the bonds?
choices: The bonds remain a liability, and no gain or loss is recognized
The bonds are derecognized and a gain or loss is recognized
The bonds are derecognized with no gain or loss
The bonds are reclassified to equity
exp: Under ASC 405-20, a liability is derecognized only if the debtor pays the creditor or is legally released; an in-substance defeasance does not qualify. Derecognizing the bonds and recognizing a gain or loss would treat the defeasance as an extinguishment.

q: On July 1, Year 1, Ames Co. issued $400,000 of 8% bonds for $427,180 to yield 6%. Interest is paid semiannually on December 31 and June 30. Using the effective interest method, what is the bonds' carrying amount at December 31, Year 1 (rounded)?
exp: Interest expense = $427,180 x 3% = $12,815; cash paid = $400,000 x 4% = $16,000; premium amortization $3,185 reduces the carrying amount to $423,995. $430,365 wrongly adds the amortization, as if the bonds were issued at a discount.

q: Rand Co., which is not experiencing financial difficulty, modified the terms of a bank loan. The present value of the cash flows under the new terms, discounted at the original effective rate, differs by 12% from the present value of the remaining cash flows under the original terms. How should Rand account for the change?
choices: As a modification, with a new effective rate applied prospectively and no gain or loss
As a troubled debt restructuring, with a gain only if undiscounted cash flows are below the carrying amount
As an extinguishment of the old debt, with the new debt recorded at fair value and a gain or loss recognized
No accounting until the debt matures
exp: Under ASC 470-50, terms are substantially different when the present value of cash flows changes by at least 10%; that is treated as an extinguishment, and the new debt is recorded at fair value with a gain or loss. Prospective modification accounting applies only below the 10% threshold.

q: During Year 1, Dale Co. recognized $46,209 of interest expense on bonds issued at a discount, and paid $40,000 of cash interest. In preparing the operating section of the statement of cash flows using the indirect method, what adjustment should Dale make to net income for the bonds?
choices: Deduct $6,209
No adjustment, because amortization relates to financing activities
exp: Discount amortization ($46,209 - $40,000 = $6,209) is a noncash part of interest expense, so it is added back to net income. Deducting it is the treatment for premium amortization, where cash paid exceeds expense.

q: On January 1, Year 1, Nash Co. borrowed $100,000 at 8%, repayable in 5 equal annual installments of $25,046 at each December 31. What amount should Nash report as the current portion of the loan at December 31, Year 1 (rounded)?
exp: Year 1 principal repaid is $25,046 - $8,000 = $17,046, leaving $82,954. Year 2 interest is $82,954 x 8% = $6,636, so the principal due within one year is $25,046 - $6,636 = $18,410. $17,046 is the Year 1 principal reduction, and $25,046 includes interest that is not yet a liability.

q: A company that elected the fair value option for its notes payable determined that the notes' fair value decreased by $50,000 during the year. Of that decrease, $20,000 was attributable to a deterioration in the company's own credit risk. How should the change be reported?
choices: Gain of $50,000 in net income
Gain of $30,000 in net income and gain of $20,000 in other comprehensive income
Gain of $20,000 in net income and gain of $30,000 in other comprehensive income
Gain of $50,000 in other comprehensive income
exp: A decrease in a liability's fair value is a gain. The $20,000 caused by instrument-specific credit risk goes to OCI, and the remaining $30,000 goes to net income (ASC 825-10-45-5). Reversing the two amounts misidentifies which part is credit-related.

q: Tate Co. had a $1,000,000 note payable due February 15, Year 2. On February 15, Year 2, Tate repaid the note from cash on hand. On March 1, Year 2, before its December 31, Year 1 statements were issued, Tate issued $1,000,000 of 10-year bonds to replenish its cash. How should the note be classified at December 31, Year 1?
choices: Noncurrent, because long-term debt was issued before the statements were issued
Noncurrent to the extent of the new long-term borrowing
Current liability
Excluded from the balance sheet, because it was repaid before issuance
exp: When a short-term obligation is repaid with current assets after the balance sheet date and long-term debt is issued later, the obligation remains current because current assets were used to settle it (ASC 470-10-45). The later borrowing did not refinance the note.

q: When is it acceptable under U.S. GAAP to amortize a bond discount using the straight-line method instead of the effective interest method?
choices: Whenever bonds are issued at a premium rather than a discount
Only for private companies that elect a practical expedient
Only for bonds with maturities of five years or less
When the results are not materially different from the effective interest method
exp: ASC 835-30-35-4 requires the interest method but permits other methods, such as straight-line, if the results are not materially different. There is no premium/discount, maturity, or private-company exception.

q: Polk Co. retired bonds with a face amount of $500,000, unamortized premium of $12,000, and unamortized debt issuance costs of $4,000 by paying 101. What gain or loss should Polk recognize?
choices: Gain of $7,000
Loss of $5,000
Gain of $3,000
Gain of $11,000
exp: Net carrying amount = $500,000 + $12,000 - $4,000 = $508,000; reacquisition price = $505,000; gain = $3,000. $7,000 ignores the unamortized issuance costs, which are part of the debt's net carrying amount.

q: Sloan Co., in financial difficulty, settled a note with a carrying amount of $380,000 by issuing 10,000 shares of its $1 par common stock with a fair value of $30 per share. What gain on restructuring should Sloan recognize?
exp: In an equity-for-debt settlement, the stock is recorded at fair value ($300,000) and the gain is the carrying amount of debt less that fair value: $380,000 - $300,000 = $80,000 (ASC 470-60). $370,000 wrongly uses the par value of the shares.
